native_dataset.database: Nonmarine Ostracod Distribution in Europe Database
native_dataset.datasetnotes: This Ostracoda dataset was uploaded as part of the bulk import of NODE (Non-marine Ostracod Distribution in Europe) to Neotoma in 2026, using the DataBUS upload system (https://github.com/NeotomaDB/DataBUS). This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

native_dataset.datasetnotes: This Ostracoda dataset was uploaded as part of the bulk import of NODE (Non-marine Ostracod Distribution in Europe) to Neotoma in 2026, using the DataBUS upload system (https://github.com/NeotomaDB/DataBUS). This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

This database import was coordinated by Alison Smith, David Horne, Robin Smith, Andrew Anderson, Simon Goring, Socorro Dominguez, and Jack Williams. David Horne is the lead steward for the NODE database which was originally established by members of the EU Human Capital and Mobility Programme project “Evolutionary ecology of reproductive modes in non-marine Ostracoda” (1994-1996), primarily to enable mapping of sexual and parthenogenetic reproductive modes.  Further development of NODE has included continued data entry, application of taxonomic revisions, and validation exercises using Google Earth and other online resources to check, correct and refine the coordinates of every record. Each record is assigned a Validation Status colour: green (accurate), amber (as good as possible given limitations of published information) or red (uncertain or unreliable and in need of further checking). Users are advised to check the Validation Status (in Site Notes) of the data they map and consider eliminating any that are “red”. Species occurrence records are derived mainly from published literature spanning the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries and represent specimens that were (or are assumed to have been) collected alive. Taxonomic names have been updated in accordance with the global checklist of Meisch et al. (2024: https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2024.974.2767) but NODE also includes the original “Name in Reference” as given in the source of the occurrence record (see Collection Unit Notes).\nNODE records include additional metadata such as environmental classifications of sites and taxonomic/nomenclatural comments that are being prepared for future import to Neotoma.

native_site.sitedescription: Kulivatnet is a small subarctic lake in northern Norway. The lake is located within the Vågneselva, a northeast-southwest trending glacially sculpted lineament. It is situated within a small but hilly catchment area, with hills up to 120 m high.  Runoff from this catchment and from the small boggy area to the southwest supplies the lake with water.  There is a single outflow at the northeast end of the lake. Vegetation around the lake can be characterized as Betula-woodland. The dominant tree is Betula pubescens, although Pinus sylvestris and Picea abies are found planted on a small hill around the pond.  Shrubs include several species of Salix sp., along with Sorbus aucuparia.  Among the common subshrubs are Vaccinium myrtillis, Vaccinium vitis-idaea.   Chamaepericlymenum suecicum, Juniperus communis and Empetrum nigrum.  Along with numerous species of Poaceae and Cyperaceae, common herbs include Geranium cf sylvaticum.  Campanula cf rotundifolia, Solidago virgaurea, Fragaria vesca and Pedicularis sceptrum-carolinum, with members of the Fabaceae, Apiace and Schrophulariaceae.  Equisetum pratense, Eriophorum angustifolium, Bistorta vivipara and Menyanthes trifoliata grow in wetter areas near and along the shore.

native_dataset.datasetnotes:
Quantification of microscopic charred particles and dark-coloured hyphae in the pollen slides was done by a calibrated eyepiece graticule with a grid of 21 by 21 lines mounted in a 10X ocular and using a 24X objective.
This method of estimating microscopic charred particle frequencies is generally similar to the method developed independently by Clark (1982).
The charred particle concentrations are divided by the pollen concentrations of terrestrial taxa and are shown as area of microfossils per pollen (micrometer square/pollen concentration ).
